14320:
Secondhand means: not coming to you directly or originally — something that has passed through someone else first.

This one idea branches into two distinct uses, and once you understand both, you'll be equipped for every situation where this word appears.

When "secondhand" describes an object, it means that object was owned and used by at least one person before the current owner.

Think of it like a chain of hands. A brand-new item starts its life in the first pair of hands — the original owner. When that person gives it away, sells it, or donates it, the next person who gets it receives it secondhand — from the second set of hands in the chain.

Examples:

  • a secondhand car — a car someone else already drove and owned before you bought it
  • secondhand clothes — clothing worn by a previous owner
  • a secondhand phone — a phone that was somebody else's before yours
  • a secondhand bookshop — a shop that sells books already read by previous owners

What it implies about condition and value:

Secondhand things are generally cheaper than new ones. They may show signs of wear — a scratch, a faded colour, a worn edge. However, "secondhand" does not automatically mean bad quality. Many secondhand items are in excellent condition. Antiques, vintage furniture, and collector's books, for example, are often secondhand yet highly prized and expensive. The word simply tells you about the item's history (previously owned), not necessarily its quality.

Opposite: brand-new, new

When "secondhand" describes information, knowledge, news, or an experience, it means you did not witness or receive it directly yourself — it came to you through another person.

This is the opposite of firsthand, which means you personally saw, heard, or experienced something yourself.

Examples:

  • secondhand information — something you were told by someone, who may themselves have heard it from yet another person
  • a secondhand account — a description of an event told by someone who wasn't there themselves, only heard about it
  • secondhand knowledge — knowledge you got from other people's reports, not from your own direct experience
  • learning something secondhand — finding out about an event not by being there, but by hearing about it later

A concrete picture:

Imagine a road accident. The person who saw it has firsthand knowledge — they witnessed it directly. Now that person tells their friend about it. The friend now has secondhand knowledge — they know about the accident, but only because someone told them. If that friend then tells another person, that third person has knowledge that is even more removed — sometimes called thirdhand.

What it implies about reliability:

Secondhand information is often considered slightly less reliable than firsthand information. Every time something passes through a person, it may get altered — accidentally misremembered, simplified, or slightly changed in emphasis. This is not always the case (a good witness can relay information very accurately), but the word carries a gentle suggestion that you should keep in mind that this came through a middleman.

This is why, in serious situations — a court case, a news report, a medical history — people are careful to note whether information is firsthand or secondhand.

Opposite: firsthand
A Special Phrase Worth Knowing: Secondhand Smoke

This is a fixed, well-known phrase you will encounter often. Secondhand smoke refers to cigarette smoke (or smoke from any tobacco product) that a non-smoker breathes in because someone nearby is smoking.

The smoker gets the smoke firsthand — they drew it into their own lungs directly. The person sitting next to them gets it secondhand — it has already passed through the smoker and into the air, and now enters the bystander's lungs without them choosing to smoke.

This is considered harmful to health, which is why smoking is banned in many indoor public spaces. The word "secondhand" here perfectly captures the idea: the bystander is receiving something they never sought, indirectly, through another person's action.

Similarly, you may also hear secondhand vaping or secondhand exposure in health contexts, following the same logic.

In everyday, informal speech, you will often hear people say they feel secondhand embarrassment. This means: watching someone else do something awkward or embarrassing, and feeling embarrassed on their behalf, even though it did not happen to you.

For example, watching a stranger trip and stumble in public and feeling your own face flush with discomfort for them — that is secondhand embarrassment. You are experiencing an emotion that rightly "belongs" to that other person, but it has transferred to you indirectly. This use is entirely consistent with the core meaning: something passed through another person to reach you.

You might also see the phrases secondhand pride, secondhand anxiety, or secondhand joy used in the same informal spirit — emotions you feel vicariously, through someone else's experience.
The Thread That Connects Both Meanings

Both meanings of "secondhand" — whether about objects or information/experiences — share the same underlying logic:

Something did not come to you in its original, direct, fresh form. It passed through at least one other person or owner before reaching you.

  • A secondhand jacket was somebody else's jacket first.
  • Secondhand news was somebody else's direct experience first.
  • Secondhand smoke was somebody else's cigarette first.
  • Secondhand embarrassment was somebody else's awkward moment first.

The "second" in secondhand literally refers to being the second (or later) in the line — not the original recipient.

UseWhat it describesWhat it means
  • For objects: not new; previously owned and used by someone else
  • For information/knowledge/experience: not received directly; it came to you through another person
  • For smoke/exposure: something you receive from another person's action, not your own
  • For emotions (informal): a feeling you have vicariously, through watching or hearing about someone else

Can it come before or after a noun?
As an adjective, "secondhand" almost always appears before the noun it describes:

  • ✅ a secondhand report
  • ✅ secondhand furniture

Is it one word or hyphenated?
Both secondhand and second-hand are correct. Modern usage, especially in American English, tends to prefer the single word. You may see second-hand more often in older British texts. Both mean exactly the same thing.

Can it be used as an adverb?
Yes — "I heard about it secondhand" or "She bought the dress secondhand" — but since you asked about the adjective form, the focus here has been on its use before nouns.
14321: The word secrete has two completely separate meanings. They just happen to share the same spelling. You'll need to figure out which one is meant from the context.
Meaning 1: To produce and release a substance (biology)

When a living body — or any part of it — makes a substance inside itself and then releases it, that process is called secreting.

Think of it this way: your body is constantly working behind the scenes, quietly making fluids and chemicals that it then sends out to do a job. That act of making and releasing is secreting.

Examples:

  • Your mouth secretes saliva. Your salivary glands make saliva and release it into your mouth so you can digest food.
  • The stomach secretes acid to break down food.
  • The liver secretes bile.
  • When you're stressed, your adrenal glands secrete adrenaline into your bloodstream.
  • A snail secretes mucus to glide across surfaces.
  • Some plants secrete nectar to attract bees.

What's the key idea? The substance is produced from within the organism (or organ or gland) and then released outward from it. It's not something that was already there — the body manufactures it and sends it out.

The noun form is secretion. The act of secreting is secretion. The substance that gets secreted is also called a secretion.

"Insulin is a secretion of the pancreas." = The pancreas produces and releases insulin.

When you'll encounter this meaning: In biology, medicine, science — anything related to the body, plants, animals, or chemistry.

When a person hides something in a place where others won't easily find it, they are secreting it.

This meaning is about deliberate, careful concealment. It's not just carelessly tossing something under a bed — it carries the sense of putting something away in a place with the specific intention that it won't be discovered.

Examples:

  • The spy secreted the documents inside a hollow book.
  • She had secreted a small amount of money in a drawer for emergencies.
  • He secreted the key under a loose floorboard.
  • The thief secreted the stolen jewels in his coat lining.

How is "secrete" different from just "hide"?

"Hide" is a broad, everyday word. "Secrete" is more formal and carries a stronger suggestion of intentional concealment, often in a clever or discreet location. It paints a picture of someone carefully stashing something away. "He hid the candy" sounds casual. "He secreted the candy" sounds deliberate and stealthy.

When you'll encounter this meaning: In fiction (thrillers, spy novels, historical writing), formal or literary writing.
How to tell the two meanings apart

The context will almost always make it obvious:

  • If the subject is a body, organ, gland, animal, or plant, and something is being produced and released, it's Meaning 1.
  • If a person (or sometimes an animal) is hiding an object somewhere, it's Meaning 2.

"The gland secretes hormones." → Meaning 1 (biology)
"She secreted the letter under the mattress." → Meaning 2 (hiding)
A note on the two meanings being unrelated

It might feel strange that one word has two such different meanings. They are historically unconnected — they simply ended up with the same spelling in English over time. Don't try to find a logical link between them. Just treat them as two separate words that look identical, the way "bank" (a financial institution) and "bank" (the side of a river) are unrelated.

What's happeningWho/what does it
Meaning 1A substance is produced inside and released outGlands, organs, organisms
Meaning 2Something is carefully hidden awayA person

Both meanings involve something being "put away" in some sense — one in the bloodstream or environment, one in a secret place — but that's where any similarity ends.
14322:
When you describe someone or something as secretive, you mean that they deliberately hide information, thoughts, plans, or activities from others — and they do this as a habit or pattern, not just once.

A secretive person does not openly share what they are doing, thinking, or feeling. They keep things to themselves on purpose, and they are careful to make sure others don't find out.

The key ideas packed inside this one word are:

1. Deliberate hiding. A secretive person is not simply quiet or shy. They are actively choosing to conceal something. There is intent behind it. They know something, and they are making sure you don't.

2. It's a pattern, not a single act. Secretive describes a tendency — a repeated behavior. If someone lies to you just once, you wouldn't necessarily call them secretive. But if they consistently avoid sharing information, dodge questions, and keep others in the dark, then that is being secretive.

3. It applies to people, organizations, and behavior. You can say a person is secretive, a government is secretive, a company is secretive, or even that someone's behavior is secretive.
What It Feels Like in Real Life

Imagine you have a friend who:

  • Never tells you where they go on weekends
  • Changes the subject whenever you ask personal questions
  • Gives vague, unclear answers to avoid revealing anything
  • Acts as if sharing information about themselves is dangerous

You would naturally think: "Why is this person hiding so much? What are they not telling me?"

That friend is being secretive. There is a wall around them — not of shyness, but of deliberate concealment.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"Secretive" almost always carries a slightly negative or suspicious tone. When you call someone secretive, you're gently suggesting that there's something they don't want you to know — and that this is a little unsettling or unusual. It creates a sense of unease or distrust.

It's not a harsh insult, but it's not a compliment either. It suggests that the person is not being fully open or honest with those around them.
How Secretive Differs from Similar Words

This is where the real sharpness of the word comes through.

Secretive vs. Private
A private person simply values their personal space and doesn't like sharing personal details — and that's completely acceptable to others. There's no suspicion attached. A secretive person, on the other hand, seems to be actively hiding something specific. The difference is: private feels natural and harmless; secretive feels like something is being concealed.

Your neighbor who never talks about their family is private.
Your neighbor who sneaks in and out of the house at odd hours and avoids all eye contact is secretive.

Secretive vs. Discreet
A discreet person is careful about sharing sensitive information — but this is seen as responsible and trustworthy. It's a compliment. A secretive person hides things in a way that feels suspicious or unnecessary. Discreet = wisely careful. Secretive = suspiciously closed-off.

Secretive vs. Mysterious
Mysterious is often neutral or even romantic — it means something is hard to understand or explain, like a mysterious old house. Secretive is specifically about a person (or group) choosing to hide information. Mysterious can happen by accident; secretive is always a choice.

• "He was secretive about his plans and refused to tell anyone where he was going."
  • "The government agency was known for being secretive, rarely releasing information to the public."
  • "She had a secretive smile, as if she knew something nobody else did."
  • "His secretive nature made it difficult for his teammates to trust him."
  • "The company was secretive about its new product, even denying that it existed."

Like most adjectives, secretive can exist on a scale. Someone can be:

  • Slightly secretive — they just don't volunteer much information
  • Very secretive — they actively avoid questions and reveal almost nothing
  • Intensely secretive — they go out of their way to hide everything, sometimes even taking measures to ensure others can never find out

You can strengthen the word by saying: "He was deeply secretive," "She was notoriously secretive," or "They were famously secretive."

• Secretly (adverb) — "She secretly read his messages." (doing something in a secret manner)
  • Secretiveness (noun) — "His secretiveness annoyed everyone around him." (the quality of being secretive)
  • Secret (noun/adjective) — the root idea: information that is hidden or kept from others
Secretive means: habitually and deliberately hiding information, thoughts, or activities from others — in a way that feels closed-off, guarded, and often a little suspicious.
14323:
A sect is a group of people who share a specific set of beliefs or practices — and whose shared beliefs set them apart from a larger, more established group they originally came from or exist in contrast to.

Think of it this way: imagine a large religion with millions of followers. Over time, some people within that religion come to believe that the mainstream is getting things wrong — maybe they're misinterpreting a holy text, following the wrong rituals, or straying from the "true" path. These people form their own tighter, more distinct group around their version of the belief. That breakaway group is a sect.

A sect is always a subgroup — it exists in relation to something bigger. You don't call an entire major religion a sect. You call a branch, a splinter group, or a faction within it a sect.

Members of a sect are united by:

  • Shared belief: They agree on a specific interpretation of doctrine, scripture, or ideology that the broader group does not share.
  • A sense of distinction: They typically believe they hold the correct or purer version of the belief, while others have drifted or gone astray.
  • Shared practice: Often, they follow particular rituals, customs, or codes of conduct that mark them as different from outsiders.
  • A defined boundary: There is usually a clear sense of "us" (the sect) vs. "them" (the larger group or mainstream society).

The word sect appears most commonly in religious contexts, but it extends further.

In religion — this is by far the most common use. Almost every major religion has sects within it.

  • Islam has two major sects: Sunni and Shia. They share the core of the Islamic faith but differ on questions of leadership and certain practices that go back to the early history of Islam.
  • Christianity has hundreds of sects — groups like Quakers, Seventh-day Adventists, and many others who broke away from mainstream churches over matters of doctrine or worship.
  • Hinduism contains many sects, such as Vaishnavism and Shaivism, which differ in which deity they regard as supreme and how they worship.
  • Buddhism too has distinct sects, like Theravada and Mahayana, with different teachings and practices.

In politics — a sect can refer to a small, tight-knit faction within a larger political movement, one that holds more extreme or distinct views than the mainstream of that movement.

In philosophy — historically, philosophical schools of thought (like the Stoics, the Epicureans) were sometimes called sects, since they were groups that gathered around specific thinkers and their doctrines.
The tone and connotation of the word

This is important to understand: the word sect is not entirely neutral. Its tone can vary depending on who uses it and in what context.

Used neutrally — academics, historians, and journalists often use "sect" as a plain descriptive term, without judgment. When a historian says "the Shia sect," they simply mean this branch of Islam.

Used with a negative shade — in everyday language, calling a group a "sect" can imply it is marginal, suspicious, rigid, or fanatical. It carries a subtle suggestion that the group is deviant from what most consider normal or acceptable. This is why members of such groups often prefer to call themselves a "church," a "denomination," or a "tradition" rather than a "sect" — because "sect" can feel like an outsider's label, one that dismisses or belittles them.

So the same group might be called a "sect" by critics and a "denomination" or "community" by its own members or sympathizers. The choice of word reveals the speaker's attitude.

Understanding "sect" becomes sharper when you compare it to related words.

Sect vs. denomination
A denomination is a larger, well-established, socially recognized branch of a religion — like Catholics, Baptists, or Lutherans within Christianity. Denominations are mainstream and respected. A sect is typically smaller, newer, more marginal, and viewed with more suspicion. The line between the two can blur over time — what starts as a sect may eventually grow into a fully accepted denomination.

Sect vs. cult
This is the most important distinction. A cult is a far more extreme version. Cults are usually characterized by:

  • An all-powerful, charismatic leader who demands absolute loyalty
  • Extreme psychological control over members
  • Isolation of members from family, friends, and outside society
  • Exit being difficult or dangerous

A sect does not necessarily have any of these features. Members of a sect typically live normal lives in the wider world. The word "sect" is much milder than "cult." However, in casual speech, people sometimes use "sect" loosely to describe what is technically a cult, so the two words do overlap in informal usage.

Sect vs. religion
A religion is the whole, the full tradition — Islam, Christianity, Hinduism. A sect is a part of it, a branch. You would never call Islam itself a sect; you would call Sunni Islam or Shia Islam sects within Islam.
A few quick examples in sentences

• After a disagreement over leadership, a small sect broke away from the main church and started holding separate gatherings.
  • The Amish are a Christian sect known for their rejection of modern technology and simple, traditional way of life.
  • The political movement eventually fractured, with one sect pushing for immediate revolution and another preferring gradual reform.
  • Historians have documented dozens of Jewish sects that existed in ancient Palestine, each with its own interpretation of the law.

A sect is a distinct subgroup — most often religious, sometimes political or philosophical — that has separated itself from a larger body through its own specific beliefs or practices. It sees itself as holding a truer, purer, or more correct understanding than the mainstream. The word is factually descriptive but carries a mild negative undertone in everyday use, suggesting something marginal or unorthodox. It is less extreme than a cult and less established than a denomination, sitting somewhere between the two on the spectrum of organized belief groups.
14324:
To understand "sectarian," you first need to understand the word sect.

A sect is a smaller group of people within a larger religion (or sometimes a political movement) that has its own specific beliefs, practices, or interpretations — ones that may differ from the mainstream. Think of it this way: Islam is a religion, and within it, Sunni and Shia are sects. Christianity is a religion, and within it, Catholicism and Protestantism are sects. The members of a sect share a tight bond around their particular version of the belief system.

Now, "sectarian" is simply the adjective built from "sect." It describes anything relating to, caused by, or characteristic of a sect or the divisions between sects.

Sectarian means: belonging to, associated with, or arising from a particular sect — especially in a way that creates division, hostility, or bias against other sects.

The word almost always carries a sense of narrowness and division. When you call something sectarian, you are pointing to the fact that it is driven by loyalty to one specific group, and that this loyalty comes at the cost of fairness, openness, or peace with others.
The Two Layers of the Word

"Sectarian" has a neutral layer and a charged, negative layer. In practice, the negative layer is far more common, so it's important to understand both.

Layer 1 — Neutral (simply "relating to a sect"):
Here, the word just describes an association with a sect, without implying conflict.

  • "The school follows a sectarian curriculum" — meaning the school teaches the beliefs and practices of a particular religious sect.
  • "Sectarian traditions vary from region to region" — meaning the customs of different religious sects differ by place.

In this layer, the word is descriptive. It doesn't judge; it just identifies.

Layer 2 — Negative (narrow, divisive, hostile):
This is how the word is used in the vast majority of real-world situations. Here, "sectarian" describes attitudes, conflicts, politics, or violence that are fuelled by excessive, narrow loyalty to one sect combined with prejudice or hostility toward people of another sect.

  • "Sectarian violence broke out in the city" — meaning people of one sect attacked people of another sect because of their religious differences.
  • "His politics are purely sectarian" — meaning he only serves or cares about his own religious or ethnic community, ignoring everyone else.
What Makes Something "Sectarian"? The Key Qualities.

When something is sectarian (in the negative sense), it typically involves one or more of these qualities:

1. Narrow-mindedness: The person or group only sees the world from their sect's perspective and refuses to consider or respect others.

2. Exclusivity: Benefits, rights, or access are reserved only for members of one sect, while others are shut out.

3. Division: Sectarian forces pull communities, societies, or nations apart along religious or ideological fault lines.

4. Prejudice and bias: There is an unfair, hostile attitude toward people simply because they belong to a different sect.

5. Conflict: At its most extreme, sectarianism leads to violence, war, or persecution between groups.
Real-World Examples to Make It Click

Example 1 — Northern Ireland:
For decades, Northern Ireland experienced what is widely called a sectarian conflict — often referred to as "The Troubles." On one side were mostly Catholics (who largely wanted to unite with Ireland) and on the other were mostly Protestants (who largely wanted to remain part of the UK). The violence, bombings, and killings between these communities were driven not just by politics, but by deep religious-group hatred. This is a textbook case of sectarian violence.

Example 2 — Iraq:
After the fall of Saddam Hussein, Sunni and Shia Muslims in Iraq descended into brutal conflict. Bombings at mosques, assassinations, and mass killings based purely on which sect of Islam a person belonged to — this is sectarian violence at its deadliest.

Example 3 — A Sectarian School:
A school that only admits children of one particular religion and teaches only that religion's worldview could be described as sectarian. It is built around and serves one sect exclusively.

Example 4 — Sectarian Politics:
A politician who only fights for the interests of their own religious community — handing out jobs, housing, and resources exclusively to members of their group while ignoring others — is practicing sectarian politics. It is governance driven by group loyalty rather than fairness.
The Spectrum: From Mild to Extreme

"Sectarian" covers a wide range of severity:

Mild end: A policy that mildly favours one religious group over others. "Critics accused the government of a sectarian approach to funding religious institutions."

Middle: Deep social divisions where communities live separately, distrust each other, and rarely mix. "The city remains deeply sectarian, with the two communities living in entirely separate neighbourhoods."

Extreme end: Open violence, killings, and warfare between groups. "Sectarian massacres left thousands dead."

The word fits all these situations. Context tells you where on the spectrum a particular usage falls.

It helps to know what the word doesn't mean:

  • It does not simply mean "religious." A person can be deeply religious without being sectarian. A sectarian person is one whose religious group identity turns into hostility or division toward others.
  • It is not the same as racism, though it can overlap with it. Sectarianism is specifically about divisions rooted in religious sect or sub-group identity, not race.
  • It does not always mean violent. A school can be sectarian without anyone getting hurt.

Understanding the opposite sharpens the meaning further.

The opposite of sectarian is non-sectarian (or sometimes ecumenical, a word used specifically in religious contexts to mean promoting unity across sects and denominations). A non-sectarian hospital treats everyone equally regardless of their religion. A non-sectarian peace agreement tries to bring rival sects together. These terms represent openness, inclusion, and unity — everything that "sectarian" is not.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Sectarian describes something rooted in the narrow identity, beliefs, or interests of a particular sect — and especially describes the division, prejudice, exclusion, or conflict that arises when loyalty to one sect breeds hostility toward others.

Every time you see the word, ask yourself: Who is the sect? Who is being divided from whom? And is there hostility or bias at play? Answer those three questions, and the word will always make perfect sense in context.
14325:
Secular means "of the ordinary world, not of religion." Think of life as being divided into two zones. One zone belongs to religion — churches, temples, mosques, scripture, priests, worship. The other zone is secular — it belongs to everyday worldly life, operating completely independently of religion. If something is secular, it has no religious character, authority, or purpose whatsoever.

This one core idea — the world, as distinct from religion — is the key to understanding every use of this word.
Meaning 1: Not Religious (The Most Common Use)

In everyday language, when you call something secular, you almost always mean it has no religious connection.

A secular school teaches science, mathematics, and literature. It is not run by a church, it doesn't teach religious scripture as truth, and it doesn't favor any faith. A secular song is one written for enjoyment or artistic expression — not for worship. Think of pop music, jazz, or folk songs, as opposed to hymns or devotional chants. A secular holiday is one with no religious basis — a national independence day, for example, is secular. A secular lifestyle means a person makes decisions based on personal choice and reason, not religious rules.

The opposites of secular in this sense are religious, sacred, and spiritual.
Meaning 2: Separation of Religion from Government and Public Life

This is the political and social meaning of the word, and it's enormously important in the modern world.

When we say a country has a secular government or is a secular state, we mean the government operates independently of any religion. Its laws are not taken from any holy book. It does not officially favor or follow any religion. People of all faiths — and people of no faith — are treated equally under the law. Religion is treated as a personal and private matter, not something the state governs by or enforces.

France, India, and the United States are commonly described as secular states. Even though large numbers of their citizens may be deeply religious, their governments are designed to function without religious authority guiding policy or law.

The broader philosophy behind this — the idea that religion and government should be kept separate — is called secularism. A person who holds this belief is called a secularist.

The direct opposite of a secular government is a theocracy, where religious leaders hold political power and laws are based on religious doctrine. Historic examples include the Papal States and Taliban-controlled Afghanistan.
Meaning 3: Clergy Who Live in the World (A Church-Specific Use)

Within Christianity, the word secular has a very specific historical use that comes directly from the core idea. There are two broad types of clergy:

Secular clergy are priests who live and work among ordinary people in the world — in parishes and communities. They are "in the world," mingling with everyday life.

Regular clergy (from regula, meaning rule) are monks, nuns, and members of religious orders — like Franciscans or Benedictines — who live inside monasteries or convents, separated from everyday worldly life and bound by strict internal rules.

So a secular priest simply means a priest who is of the world — not cloistered away. This meaning connects perfectly to the core idea: secular = belonging to the world, not withdrawn from it into a purely religious enclosure.
Meaning 4: Happening Over an Extremely Long Period of Time (Scientific Use)

In science — particularly in astronomy, geology, and physics — secular takes on a different but related shade of meaning. Here it describes changes or processes that happen very slowly over extremely long periods of time, spanning centuries or even geological ages.

Secular variation in Earth's magnetic field refers to the slow, centuries-long drift of the magnetic poles. Secular cooling refers to the gradual, age-spanning decrease in the heat of Earth's interior. Secular acceleration in astronomy refers to tiny, long-term shifts in the motion of planets or moons accumulating over thousands of years.

Why does "secular" mean long-term here? Because the word connects to the idea of ages — vast stretches of worldly time. These are not quick changes. They are changes that unfold on the scale of the world's own lifespan.
Meaning 5: Long-Term Structural Trends (Economics and Finance)

Borrowed directly from the scientific use above, the word secular is now very widely used in economics and finance. Here it means a trend or condition that is deep, structural, and long-lasting — persisting for many years or decades — as opposed to a temporary, short-term swing.

A secular bull market is a long-term period, often lasting a decade or more, during which stock prices broadly rise. A secular bear market is the opposite — a prolonged stretch of stagnant or declining prices. Secular stagnation refers to a persistent, long-run slowdown in economic growth that isn't just a temporary dip but a structural condition of the economy. A secular trend in consumer behavior means a deep, lasting shift in how people spend or live — not a passing fad.

The direct contrast here is with cyclical — meaning short-term swings that go up and down in regular, repeating patterns. Secular trends persist through many cycles.

The word secular appears in very different fields, but one thread always connects its meanings:

The world. Secular always points to the world — whether it's the world as opposed to religion, the world as opposed to a monastery's walls, or the vast sweep of time across which the world itself exists.

Once you see that thread, the word becomes simple. Secular is always about this world, this life, this long span of earthly time — as distinct from the divine, the sacred, the cyclical, or the cloistered.
14326:
Imagine drawing a line through all of human life, dividing it into two zones. On one side: religion, the divine, the sacred, the spiritual. On the other side: everything else — government, courts, schools, science, public policy, everyday society. The word secular labels that second zone — the non-religious, worldly domain of human affairs.

This is the foundation. Everything else builds on it.
The Noun Forms

The word "secular" has three noun forms, each worth knowing:

  1. Secularism — the most important one; an ideology or principle
  2. Secularity — a less common form; describes a state or quality
  3. A secular — an old, now rare usage referring to a type of priest
1. Secularism

Secularism is the belief or principle that religion should be kept separate from public life — particularly from government, law, and public institutions. It says: the state should run on the basis of human reason, evidence, and civil law — not on the commands of any religious scripture, religious leader, or religious doctrine.

Here is the core argument of secularism, stated plainly:

"In a society of many different people — Hindus, Muslims, Christians, atheists, agnostics — no government should base its laws on what one group's religion says. Laws that govern everyone must come from reason and consent, not from any faith's scripture."

That's it. That's the heart of secularism.

Notice what secularism is not saying. It is not saying: "Religion is bad." It is not saying: "People should stop believing in God." It is simply saying: "Religion belongs in the personal and private sphere — in your home, your place of worship, your community. It should not control the machinery of government that rules over people of all faiths and no faith."
What Secularism Looks Like in Practice

Secularism operates across several areas of public life:

In Government and Politics

A secular state is neutral on questions of religion. It does not declare any official religion. It does not write laws based on what the Bible, the Quran, the Gita, or any other scripture says. It treats a Hindu citizen and a Muslim citizen and an atheist citizen as equal before the law, with the same rights and the same duties.

For example: a secular government would not make a law saying "you must fast on Ramadan" or "you must not eat beef" or "you must attend Sunday church" — because those are religious rules, not civil ones.

In Education

A secular school teaches subjects — science, history, mathematics, literature — using evidence-based, universally accepted frameworks. It does not teach any religion's doctrines as objective truth to all students. Evolution is taught in biology class. The historical origins of the universe are taught in physics using cosmological science.

This does not mean religion is banned from discussion. Religion can absolutely be studied as a part of history, culture, philosophy, or comparative religion. The difference is: studying a religion academically is very different from imposing a religion as truth on students of all backgrounds.

In Courts and Law

A secular legal system applies laws written by human legislatures and interpreted by trained judges. It does not apply religious law — like Sharia (Islamic law) or Canon Law (Catholic church law) — over citizens who may not follow that religion.

In Society

In a secular society, religious practice is considered a personal, private matter. You are completely free to pray, go to your mosque or temple or church, follow your religious customs in your home and community. But the shared public space — the parliament, the courtroom, the government hospital — is neutral ground where no single religion's rules govern everyone.
What Secularism Is NOT

This is crucial, because secularism is frequently misunderstood.

Secularism is not atheism. An atheist does not believe in God. A secularist may be deeply, personally religious. Mahatma Gandhi was profoundly religious — he prayed daily and was guided by Hindu and Christian texts — but he strongly believed the Indian state should not favor Hinduism or any other religion. That position is secularism. Many deeply religious people are also committed secularists, because they believe everyone's religion (including their own) deserves protection from state interference.

Secularism is not anti-religion. It does not want to destroy religion, mock it, or eliminate it. It simply wants religion to operate in its own sphere — personal faith, religious communities, places of worship — without commanding political authority over those who don't share it.

Secularism is not irreligion. "Irreligion" means having no religious belief. Secularism is about institutional separation, not personal belief. The two are entirely different things. A society can be full of deeply religious people and still be secular in its institutions.
2. Secularity

"Secularity" refers to the quality or condition of being secular — how thoroughly an institution, society, or culture has separated from religious influence. It's a more abstract noun.

If someone says "the secularity of French public life is very strong," they mean French public institutions are very thoroughly separated from religious control and influence. If someone says "the secularity of a country's court system," they mean how free that court system is from religious law and religious authority.

It describes a degree or state rather than a belief or movement. You might say: "The secularity of Scandinavian countries is high," meaning those countries operate with very little religious influence in their public institutions.
3. A Secular (The Older Noun Usage)

This is a historical usage, mostly found in older texts, religious history, and literature. It is rare in everyday modern conversation but worth knowing.

In Catholic Church history, the clergy was traditionally divided into two categories:

Regular clergy: Priests and monks who belonged to a religious order — like the Franciscans, Dominicans, or Jesuits. They lived in monasteries under strict communal rules. They were called "regular" because they followed a rule (a strict set of regulations governing monastic life).

Secular clergy: Priests who lived and worked in the world — serving ordinary parishes, ministering to communities in towns and villages, under the authority of a local bishop. They were called "secular" because they operated in the ordinary, everyday world, not in the closed world of a monastery.

So "a secular" (used as a noun) referred to a secular priest — a parish priest who lived and ministered among ordinary people. Sometimes the term also extended to refer to a layperson — someone who is not part of the clergy at all.

Today, this usage mainly appears in historical, theological, or literary contexts. You are unlikely to hear it in everyday speech.
Why Did Secularism Emerge?

Understanding where secularism came from makes the idea much clearer.

For most of European history, the Catholic Church held enormous power over governments. Kings and queens needed the Pope's blessing and approval. Laws were rooted in church doctrine. Heresy — disagreeing with church teachings — was a crime punishable by death. Minority religious groups (Jews, Protestants, Muslims) faced persecution under state enforcement of religious rules.

Over time, as societies grew more diverse, as science emerged, and as philosophy matured, thinkers began arguing: a government serving all its people cannot be the instrument of one religion. The state must be a neutral entity that protects everyone's freedom — including freedom of religion and freedom from imposed religion.

This produced the idea of secularism: separating the church and the state, protecting individuals from theocracy (government by religious authority), and ensuring that laws are made through reason and democratic consent, not through religious edicts.
Secularism Around the World

Secularism is not an all-or-nothing condition. Countries exist on a wide spectrum.

France practices one of the strictest forms of secularism, called laïcité (the French word for secularity). Religious symbols — like headscarves or large crosses — are banned for teachers and officials in public schools and government buildings. Religion is considered strictly private.

The United States has a strong secular framework in its Constitution. The First Amendment prohibits the government from establishing any official religion and protects the free practice of religion. However, religion is very active in American public culture and political discourse — which creates ongoing tensions about where the line falls.

The United Kingdom has a moderate, somewhat inconsistent form of secularism. The Church of England is technically the official state church, the monarch is its head, and 26 Church of England bishops sit in the House of Lords. Yet religious doctrine does not directly govern most lawmaking, and all religions are legally equal.

Saudi Arabia is explicitly not secular. The legal system is based on Sharia (Islamic law), religious authorities have significant political power, and the state actively enforces religious observance.

India officially declares itself a "secular republic" in its constitution, meaning the state has no official religion and must treat all religions equally. In practice, what this means and how it is implemented is one of the most hotly debated political questions in modern India.
Secular Humanism

This is an important related concept worth knowing.

Secular humanism is a specific philosophy that combines secularism with humanism — the belief that human beings, guided by reason, evidence, and empathy, can create ethical, meaningful, and flourishing lives without reference to God or religion. Secular humanists believe that morality, purpose, and social good can be derived from reason and human experience rather than from divine command.

It is worth noting: secular humanism is a specific philosophical stance (and tends toward atheism or agnosticism), whereas secularism by itself is simply about institutional separation and is compatible with personal religious belief.
Secularization (A Related Process)

There is also the word secularization, which refers to the historical or social process by which a society, institution, or culture gradually moves away from religious authority and toward secular frameworks. For example, when universities in medieval Europe were controlled by the Church, and over centuries became independent academic institutions governed by academic freedom — that shift is called secularization.
Quick Summary

Here is everything in brief:

Secularism — The principle that religion and the state should be separate; that public life, law, and government should be governed by reason and civil authority rather than by any religion's doctrine. It protects both religious freedom (no state can tell you what to believe) and civil equality (no one's religion can be imposed on others through law).

Secularity — The quality or state of being secular; how thoroughly an institution or society has separated from religious influence.

A secular — An old noun referring to a parish priest (not a monastic one) or a layperson. Mostly historical.

Secularization — The gradual process by which societies or institutions move away from religious authority.

Secular humanism — A philosophy combining secularism with the belief that human reason and empathy are sufficient guides for a good life, without religion.

The key insight to hold onto: secular does not mean hostile to religion. It means neutral toward religion in the public sphere — a space of equal treatment where no single faith holds political authority over others.
14327: "Secure" means free from danger, doubt, or the risk of something going wrong. Whether you're talking about a building, a physical object, a job, or a feeling inside a person — when something is secure, it is safe, stable, and not easily threatened or lost. The simplest way to remember it: if something is secure, you don't have to worry about it.

1. Protected from danger or threat

When a place or situation is described as secure, it means it is guarded and protected — harmful things cannot easily reach it. A secure building keeps intruders out. A secure location keeps valuables safe. A secure border is one that is well-defended. The idea here is always about external threats being kept away. "The embassy is in a secure compound." "Keep the documents in a secure place."

2. Firmly fixed and not likely to move or fall

When a physical object is secure, it means it is fastened tightly and won't slip, shake, loosen, or collapse. This is the most physical, tangible sense of the word. "Check that the knot is secure before you climb." "The shelf brackets must be secure before you load any weight on them." "Is the car seat secure?" Here, the opposite of secure is loose, wobbly, or unstable.

3. Certain, stable, and not at risk of disappearing

This meaning applies to life situations — jobs, futures, positions, and relationships — that are solid and reliable. They are not fragile; you can count on them. "She has a secure job" means she is not in danger of being fired anytime soon. "He wants a secure future for his family" means a future that is guaranteed and protected from uncertainty. "The team's place in the competition is secure" means they cannot be knocked out. The opposite here is precarious — something that feels unstable and could collapse at any moment.

4. Emotionally confident and at peace with yourself

This is perhaps the most human and personal meaning. A person who is emotionally secure feels calm, confident, and safe from within. They don't constantly need reassurance from others, they are not easily shaken by criticism or jealousy, and they have a stable sense of who they are. "She is a very secure person — she doesn't need others' approval to feel good about herself." "The child felt secure whenever his mother was nearby." "He is completely secure in his identity." The direct opposite of this is insecure — someone who doubts themselves, feels threatened by others, or constantly seeks validation.
The Thread That Connects All Four Meanings

Even though the four meanings seem different on the surface, they all point to the same underlying feeling: the absence of threat, risk, or worry. A secure building is not threatened by intruders. A secure rope is not threatened by loosening. A secure job is not threatened by loss. A secure person is not threatened by doubt. No matter the context, "secure" always signals that something is stable and protected.

"Secure" is a gradable adjective, meaning it can exist on a scale. You can say something is more secure, less secure, relatively secure, or highly secure. Nothing in the real world is ever completely and perfectly secure — there is always some degree of risk. So context matters a great deal. A bank vault is more secure than a shoebox, but even a vault isn't impenetrable.

Knowing the word alone is not enough — you also need to know how it lives in real sentences alongside other words.

"Secure in the knowledge that..." means to feel calm and confident because you know something is handled or true. "She left for the trip, secure in the knowledge that her team would take care of everything." It's a lovely, slightly formal expression.

"Financially secure" means having enough money and stability that you don't have to worry about paying bills or facing poverty. It's one of the most common collocations of the word.

"Emotionally secure" refers specifically to that inner confidence described in Meaning 4 — a calm, stable sense of self.

"Secure attachment" is a term from psychology that describes a healthy emotional bond — especially between a child and a parent — where the child feels consistently loved, safe, and cared for. Children with secure attachment tend to grow into more confident adults.

"A secure connection" or "a secure website" is a technology term meaning that the data being transferred is encrypted and protected from hackers. When you see "https" in a web address, that "s" stands for secure.

"A secure facility" means a heavily guarded, restricted place — like a prison, a military base, or a government installation.

"Secure" vs. "safe": These words are close but not identical. Safe usually describes a condition right now — "You are safe here." Secure suggests an ongoing, built-in state of protection or stability — "This is a secure environment." Safe is about the present moment; secure is about a sustained condition over time.

Secure does not mean perfect. Calling something secure is not a guarantee that nothing bad will ever happen — it just means the risk is low and protections are in place. Even the most secure systems in the world have vulnerabilities.

Secure does not mean arrogant. An emotionally secure person is not boastful, aggressive, or dismissive of others. They are simply calm and grounded. Confidence without anxiety — that is what emotional security looks like.

The most natural antonym of "secure" is insecure — a loose bolt, a job that could end any day, or a person who constantly doubts themselves are all insecure. Other antonyms, depending on the context, include vulnerable (open to attack or harm), precarious (dangerously unstable), shaky (physically or figuratively), at risk, and uncertain.

"Secure" is a richly layered word, but it is always doing the same job: it tells you that something or someone is protected, stable, dependable, and free from the threat of harm, loss, or collapse. Whether the subject is a locked vault, a tightly tied knot, a steady career, or a person's inner sense of self — to be secure is to stand on solid ground.
14328: At the heart of every use of "secure" as a verb is one powerful idea: taking something uncertain, unstable, or at risk, and making it certain, stable, and safe. All its meanings are expressions of this single core.
Meaning 1: To fasten or fix something firmly in place

When you secure something physically, you attach or fix it so that it cannot move, slip, fall, or come loose. The action removes physical instability.

Think of a sailor securing a boat to a dock with a rope — tying it tight so it doesn't drift away. Or a worker securing heavy cargo in a truck with straps so it doesn't slide around during transit.

"Secure the lid before you shake the bottle."
"The climber secured the rope to the rock face before descending."
"She secured her luggage to the roof rack."

The test for this meaning: if you can physically touch and fix the thing in place, this is the meaning at work.
Meaning 2: To protect something from danger, attack, or threat

To secure a place or thing means to make it safe — to guard it against intruders, harm, theft, or any kind of risk. This is the meaning behind the word "security." You are actively setting up protection so that nothing bad can get in or happen.

This sense is widely used in military, law enforcement, and everyday safety contexts.

"Police secured the crime scene so no one could disturb the evidence."
"The army secured the border crossing."
"He secured his home before leaving for a month — locked everything, set the alarm."
"The company secured its network against hackers."

The difference from Meaning 1: here, you are not stopping something from falling — you are stopping a threat from entering or causing harm.

Meaning 3: To successfully obtain or achieve something (often after effort or competition)

This is the most commonly used meaning in everyday English, especially in professional and formal contexts. When you secure a job, a deal, a loan, or a victory, it means you have successfully obtained or achieved it — often after working hard, competing for it, or going through a formal process. The word implies not just that you have it, but that it is now confirmed and locked in.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "I got a job at the firm."
  • "I secured a job at the firm."

Both mean you obtained the job. But "secured" carries a stronger, more deliberate feeling — it suggests effort, competition, or a formal process was involved, and that the outcome is now certain and yours.

"She secured a full scholarship to study abroad."
"The company secured a multimillion-dollar contract."
"He secured funding for his startup after months of pitching to investors."
"The team secured a place in the finals."
Meaning 4: To make a future outcome certain or guaranteed

Closely related to Meaning 3, this use focuses on locking in a result — making something that was uncertain become definite. You are not obtaining a thing so much as guaranteeing what will happen.

"Winning tonight will secure their championship title."
"Getting this signature secures your legal rights to the property."
"That performance secured her reputation as one of the best in her field."

In each case, one action makes a future result a certainty rather than a possibility.

Meaning 5 (Financial/Legal): To back a loan with an asset as a guarantee

In finance and law, "to secure a loan" means to support or guarantee it using something of value — called collateral. The asset acts as the lender's safety net: if the borrower cannot repay, the lender can legally take the asset. The asset is what "secures" the loan — it is the guarantee that removes the lender's risk.

"The loan was secured against his house." — If he fails to repay, the bank can claim the house.
"A secured credit card requires a cash deposit as collateral."
"The business loan was secured using the company's equipment."

An unsecured loan, by contrast, has no such collateral backing it — which is why unsecured loans typically carry higher interest rates. The lender takes on more risk.

As a verb, "secure" is transitive — meaning it always needs an object. You always secure something. You cannot just say "he secured." You must say "he secured the door" or "she secured a deal."

It is also commonly used in the passive voice, especially in formal writing:

"The funds have been secured."
"The area was secured by police."
"A deal was secured after weeks of negotiation."
The One Idea Behind All Five Meanings

Though the contexts differ widely — tying down a rope, guarding a building, winning a contract, guaranteeing an outcome, or backing a loan — every use of "secure" as a verb removes some form of uncertainty, instability, or risk.

Something that was loose becomes fixed. Something that was vulnerable becomes protected. Something that was uncertain becomes confirmed. Something that was at risk becomes guaranteed.

That is the verb "secure" in its entirety — making things firm, safe, and certain.
14329: The word sedan, used as a noun, has two distinct meanings — one modern and very common, and one historical.
Meaning 1: A Type of Car (the modern meaning)

A sedan is a specific style of passenger car. It is probably the most common and "standard" type of car you see on roads.

What it looks like

A sedan has three clearly separate sections when you look at it from the side:

  1. The front hood — covering the engine.
  2. The passenger cabin — the enclosed area where people sit, with windows on all sides and a fixed, solid roof.
  3. The trunk (also called the boot in British English) — a completely enclosed storage compartment at the rear.

Each of these three sections is visually distinct — you can see three separate "boxes" making up the shape of the car. This is why car designers and engineers sometimes call a sedan a "three-box car."

Key features

  • It has a fixed, solid roof that cannot be folded or removed.
  • The trunk is fully enclosed and separate from the passenger cabin. If you're sitting in the back seat, you cannot reach into the trunk — there is no opening between them (unlike some other car types).
  • It typically has four doors — two on the left side and two on the right. Some sedans have only two doors, but four-door sedans are far more common.
  • It usually seats four to five passengers comfortably.

How it differs from other car types

Understanding what a sedan is becomes much clearer when you compare it to cars it is often confused with:

Sedan vs. Hatchback:
A hatchback also has four doors and looks similar to a sedan, but the key difference is the rear. In a hatchback, the rear window is part of a large door that swings upward, and the cargo/luggage area flows directly into the passenger cabin — they are one connected space. In a sedan, the trunk is a completely separate, closed-off compartment. If you open the trunk of a sedan, you're opening a separate lid, not a door connected to the cabin.

Sedan vs. SUV (Sport Utility Vehicle):
An SUV is much taller, sits higher off the ground, has a bigger body, and its cargo area is part of the same interior space as the passengers. SUVs are built for more rugged use and offer more interior room. A sedan is lower, sleeker, and more fuel-efficient.

Sedan vs. Coupe:
A coupe is a car with a sportier, lower roofline and typically only two doors. It also usually has less rear headroom. A sedan prioritizes practicality and space for four or more people; a coupe prioritizes style.

Sedan vs. Convertible:
A convertible has a roof that can be folded back or removed entirely, exposing passengers to the open sky. A sedan always has a fixed, permanent roof.

Sedan vs. Station Wagon (also called an Estate):
A station wagon extends the roofline all the way to the back of the car, creating a large cargo area that connects with the passenger cabin. A sedan's roofline drops down before the trunk, leaving a separate enclosed boot.

Why sedans are popular

Sedans are considered the "classic" car shape for a reason. They offer a good balance of:

  • Practicality — a separate, secure trunk keeps luggage out of the cabin.
  • Comfort — the enclosed cabin is quiet, and the fixed roof provides structural strength.
  • Fuel efficiency — their lower, aerodynamic shape tends to consume less fuel compared to taller vehicles like SUVs.
  • Ease of use — four doors make it easy for everyone to get in and out.

They are widely used as family cars, taxis, company cars, and everyday commuter vehicles all over the world.

In British English

In British English and in some other varieties of English, a sedan is called a saloon or saloon car. The two words refer to the exact same type of vehicle. If you read British automotive journalism, you'll see "saloon" where Americans would write "sedan."

Example sentences

  • "He drove a black sedan to the airport."
  • "I prefer a sedan over an SUV because it's easier to park."
  • "The police chased the getaway sedan down the highway."
Meaning 2: A Sedan Chair (the historical meaning)

Before cars existed, the word sedan referred to something completely different — a sedan chair, which was an enclosed, chair-like cabin used as a form of transport for people.

What it was

A sedan chair was essentially a small, box-shaped cabin just large enough for one seated person. It had a door, windows (sometimes with curtains for privacy), and a seat inside. The cabin was mounted on two long horizontal poles that extended out from the front and the back.

Two men called bearers or porters carried this chair — one person at the front holding the poles and one at the back. The passenger sat inside, completely enclosed, while the bearers walked and transported them from one place to another.

When and where it was used

Sedan chairs were used primarily in 17th and 18th century Europe, especially in cities like London and Paris. They were a popular and fashionable way for wealthy people to travel through busy city streets without getting muddy, wet, or jostled by crowds.

They were especially useful in narrow medieval city streets where carriages pulled by horses could not easily fit. A sedan chair only needed the width of two men walking.

Over time, as wheeled vehicles like proper horse-drawn carriages and eventually automobiles became widespread, the sedan chair became obsolete and disappeared from everyday use.

Today, sedan chairs are mostly seen in museums, historical films, or period dramas set in earlier centuries.

Example sentences

  • "The noblewoman arrived at the palace in a sedan."
  • "Sedan chairs were a common sight in 18th century London."

In virtually all modern, everyday usage, sedan refers to the car. If someone says "she bought a sedan" or "it was a white sedan," they are always talking about the car. The historical meaning (the carried chair) only comes up in historical writing, literature, or discussions of the past.
